title: Beijing's $14bn Taiwan Arms Package Stalls as Trump Courts Xi, While the Kremlin Calls the Ukraine Peace Draft Thin and France Bans Saturday Protests
subhead: Taiwan has waited months for Washington to clear a $14 billion package of Patriots, command systems and a 360-degree radar for its T-Dome air defence, and US officials now say the sale is likely to be split into smaller tranches to protect the trade truce with Xi Jinping. Separately, the Kremlin dismissed the latest Ukraine proposals as lacking substance even as it agreed in principle to three-way talks in mid-November, and Paris moved to ban unauthorised demonstrations ahead of a second weekend of unrest.

sections.heading: Taiwan's Air Defence Package Is Stuck Behind the US-China Truce
sections.body:
AFP reported on Friday that Taiwan has been waiting months for President Donald Trump to approve a $14 billion sale of US weapons and equipment. The package includes Patriot missiles, an automated command and control system and a 360-degree air defence radar, which Su Tzu-yun of Taipei's Institute for National Defense and Security Research described as components that together could strengthen Taiwan's strategic air defence. Money for it is expected to come from a $25 billion defence spending bill Taiwan's parliament passed in May. Washington approved a record $11.1 billion package in December.

The delay is political. Trump and Xi Jinping met in Beijing in May, and AFP reports that Xi warned Washington that missteps on Taiwan could push the two countries into conflict; Trump later said arms sales to Taiwan could be a bargaining chip with China. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in June the package was under review, and officials had also been assessing whether US stockpiles were sufficient for its Iran operations. A US official told AFP that the chances of the package being split into smaller chunks have gone way up.

In Taipei's own accounting, the gap is getting dangerous. Taiwan's defence ministry said on Friday that it tracked three Chinese naval vessels and seven official ships around the island in the 24 hours to 6am, though no aircraft were detected, according to the state Central News Agency. Taiwanese forces also ran coastal missile drills in Kaohsiung this week. 'Militarily, Taiwan is racing against time,' Su said. 'Acquiring weapons is not like ordering at a drive-through.'
sections.whyItMatters: The Taiwan arms pipeline is now being priced by Washington as trade leverage rather than deterrence. Every month of delay moves delivery and training further out, and the option of splitting the package into tranches would let the White House sell the same deterrent twice while Beijing watches.

sections.heading: The Kremlin Calls the Ukraine Draft Thin, Then Agrees to Talk in November
sections.body:
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday that Russia was in principle ready to resume trilateral talks in mid-November, after the US midterm elections, and that Moscow wanted them to focus on postwar security, the Guardian reported. He said Witkoff had briefed Putin on new aspects in the approaches of the Europeans and Kyiv from the Oslo meeting, but that there wasn't really much substance in them. Witkoff called the talks constructive while conceding there is still important work to do; Zelensky said Kyiv backs resuming talks as soon as possible, while AP reported the Kremlin's account as agreement to resume three-way talks.

Trump nonetheless claimed the process was the closest we've been to ending the war. The diplomacy is already entangled in Washington's domestic politics: Witkoff drew sharp criticism, including from Republican senator Thom Tillis, for calling Putin a humanitarian after Moscow released US citizen Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old former teacher held for more than four years. Vice-President JD Vance defended the remark.

The fighting has not paused. Missiles struck Kyiv in the early hours of Thursday, wounding 15 people and damaging subway infrastructure on the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro, per Ukrainian authorities; a Russian strike in Kharkiv region killed a woman, and a drone hit energy infrastructure near Kremenchuk. Moscow's mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 630 drones were sent toward the capital overnight, with two people wounded near Moscow. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said appeasement and flattery would not stop Russia, and separately, Rubio said decisions on Ukraine's access to Starlink rest with SpaceX rather than the White House — comments that followed a Wall Street Journal report that Musk had slowed a military-grade Starlink service Ukraine relies on for missile defence.
sections.whyItMatters: Moscow has agreed to a date without agreeing to terms, and it set the date after the US midterms. That sequencing gives Russia leverage over what Washington puts on the table, while Ukraine's two most sensitive dependencies — Starlink and Patriot-class interceptors — are both being rationed by Washington and its contractors.

sections.heading: France Bans Protests and Extends Curfews Before a Second Weekend
sections.body:
President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday that illegitimate protests would be banned in the coming days, after meeting intelligence chiefs and senior ministers at the Elysée, RFI reported. Trade union marches may proceed on diverted routes, but everything else, where possible, is being prohibited. The government blamed last Saturday's riots and looting on ultra-left groups; Macron described political and seditious acts aimed at bringing down the Republic.

The measures are sweeping. All Saturday protests in Lyon are banned, and marches planned for Thursday in Paris, Lyon, Lille and Grenoble were also banned — the Paris ban covers the Elysée, both houses of parliament, the Louvre and the Champs-Elysées. The BBC reported that Paris extended a partial curfew in Place de la République and the Les Halles area until Monday, that the Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums will close on Saturday, and that Marseille and Lyon imposed total protest bans for the weekend. Public transport in Marseille is suspended on Saturday and an overnight curfew will cover the entire population.

The numbers show the scale. Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said on Wednesday that about 2,500 people had been taken into custody, 174 jailed and 917 formally prosecuted; by Thursday the BBC, citing him, put arrests at 2,700 and jailings at 217, with more than 1,000 brought to court and half of those detained having no prior record. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, who has admitted police lost control during the violence, said deployments would rise 20% versus last weekend. Central Paris shops are boarding up windows and Hermès has increased security at its French stores.
sections.whyItMatters: A G7 state is governing a cost-of-living protest wave with curfews, protest bans and mass fast-track prosecutions. The trigger is prices — the same energy shock now pushing Brent above $113 — so the political damage in Europe is being imported from the Gulf.

sections.heading: Oil Settles Above $113 as the Gulf Risk Premium Outlives the Hormuz Recovery
sections.body:
ICE Brent settled 4% higher at just above $113 a barrel on Thursday, its highest since May 4, and was trading at $112.96 in early Asian hours on Friday; WTI was near $98-99 after a 2.4% jump, Arab News and CNBC-TV18 reported. ING's commodities desk noted the rally is driven less by current fundamentals than by fear of renewed escalation in the Persian Gulf, and that its earlier expectation of Brent averaging $80 in the fourth quarter now looks unattainable. Brent is set for a third consecutive weekly gain while WTI is on track to end a two-week run higher.

The physical market is telling a different story. CNBC-TV18 reported that Dated Brent, the physical barrel, has fallen nearly $15 in two weeks towards $120, as Gulf supplies resume and freight rates cool — a widening gap between futures pricing a war and cargoes pricing a recovery. Diesel has hit record highs in the US, prompting a deal with Russia for diesel supply and a 60-day sanctions waiver. Libya shut a pipeline valve from the Hamada and Tahara fields to Zawiya port, cutting production, the National Oil Corporation chief told Reuters.

On the military side the signals point two ways. The IRGC said its navy struck four violating ships in the central Gulf and that three other vessels exploded after hitting mines west of Hormuz, per Sepah News. Trump told reporters on Thursday the US has knocked out Iran and threatened to go a little bit further, while a New York Times report cited by CNBC-TV18 says the US and Israel have plans for renewed strikes after the November 3 midterms. ING also reported a second US aircraft carrier heading to the region, alongside reports that US troops have been evacuated from some Middle East bases.
sections.whyItMatters: The premium in futures is now a bet on what happens after the US midterms, not on today's flows. European gas tells the same story: TTF settled above EUR90/MWh, its highest since December 2022, with EU storage peaking just under 75% — a thin buffer going into winter if Gulf LNG does not return.

sections.heading: Sudan Denies the Abyei Market Strike as Both Sides Demand an Investigation
sections.body:
Sudan's foreign ministry said on Thursday that the Sudanese Armed Forces had absolutely no connection to the October 19 drone attack on Amiet Common Market in Abyei, a trading centre serving the Ngok Dinka and Misseriya communities, Radio Tamazuj reported. The ministry offered no evidence and did not describe the circumstances of the attack; it instead accused the RSF of other strikes, including a December 2025 assault on a UN peacekeeping camp in Kadugli that it said killed members of the Bangladeshi contingent.

Abyei officials initially reported at least 73 dead and 19 wounded, then raised the toll to 153, with victims including Sudanese, South Sudanese and foreign nationals buried in two mass graves. South Sudan summoned Sudan's ambassador in Juba to protest. The RSF-aligned Government of Peace said it filed a complaint on October 19 with the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for Sudan through the UN human rights office, asking investigators to establish circumstances, determine criminal responsibility, preserve evidence and protect witnesses; its foreign minister, Ammar Amoun Deldoum, said there had been no military presence in the demilitarised area and urged UNISFA to document evidence.
sections.whyItMatters: Abyei is the seam between two states and a UN-mandated demilitarised zone, and a mass-casualty drone strike there has now produced competing war-crimes filings rather than a joint inquiry. Both Khartoum and the RSF's rival administration are courting the same UN mechanism, which means the fight over attribution is now as important as the battlefield.

sections.heading: Putin Reshuffles His Government as Washington Talks to Moscow
sections.body:
Vladimir Putin signed decrees on Thursday appointing four deputy prime ministers, a new transport minister and a presidential aide, all effective on signing, Xinhua reported. Irina Okladnikova, formerly deputy finance minister, becomes deputy prime minister and chief of government staff; Oleg Kozhemyako, governor of Primorsky Krai, becomes deputy prime minister and presidential plenipotentiary envoy to the Far Eastern Federal District; and Andrei Nikitin, who had headed the transport ministry, becomes deputy prime minister.

The reshuffle lands days before US-Russia technical talks resume and weeks before a possible trilateral round. Two of the four promotions are economic and logistics figures — finance and transport — while the Far East posting puts a former governor with security credentials in charge of Russia's Pacific-facing region, where Japan's new missile deployments on Yonaguni and North Korean ties are both live issues.
sections.whyItMatters: Personnel changes are one of the few reliable signals of what a Kremlin expects to need. Elevating finance and transport officials while the US offers talks suggests Moscow is preparing for a long war economy and a rebuilt logistics chain, not for a settlement that would make either redundant.

bottomLine: The day's most consequential move was a non-move: Washington let a $14 billion Taiwan air defence package sit for months and signalled it may be broken into pieces, using Taipei's deterrent as a chip in the trade truce with Xi. Moscow, meanwhile, accepted a mid-November date for three-way talks only after saying the European and Ukrainian ideas had little substance, and kept striking Kyiv through it. Oil above $113 has already reached European politics, where France is deploying curfews and protest bans against a cost-of-living revolt before Saturday. The pattern across all three fronts is that escalation and diplomacy are running on separate clocks — the military ones set by Washington and Moscow, the political ones set by elections and by prices.
